newsitem.title: UK: Simple test can point to drinking problems.
newsitem.headline: Simple test can point to drinking problems.

text.p: Italian doctors said on Friday that a simple five-question test could be used to see if patients had drinking problems -- and it worked as well as longer tests.
Marco Piccinelli and colleagues at the University of Verona tried out the tests on 480 volunteers at various clinics.
They gave them a 10-question test aimed at evaluating potential alcohol abuse that has been issued by the World Health Organisation.

They analysed the answers and then used statistics to see if some of the questions could be omitted without affecting the outcome. They came up with a five-question version that predicted alcohol problems almost as well.

"Using five of the 10 items on the questionnaire gives reasonable accuracy, and these are recommended as questions of choice to screen patients for alcohol problems," they wrote in a report in the British Medical Journal. The questions included how often people had a drink, how many drinks a day they had, how often they were unable to stop drinking once started, how often they had "failed to do what was normally expected" because of drinking, and whether a friend, relative, or doctor had ever expressed concern about drinking.
A drink was defined as one glass (125 ml or 4 oz) of wine, one beer (500 ml or 8 oz) or one 40 ml measure of spirits.

Hazardous alcohol intake is defined as three to seven drinks almost every day, or seven or more drinks three times a week, in men. In women it is two to five drinks almost every day or five or more drinks at least three times a week.

Alcohol dependence or harmful use of alcohol is seen in about six percent of patients seeking treatment from a general practitioner -- making it the third most common psychological problem after depression and general anxiety.
